title: 07. Google ADK: Day 9 — Memory Service & Artifacts — Long-term Storage
summary: Cross-session semantic recall with Memory, and versioned binary storage with Artifacts
objectives: Mermaid — Memory + Artifact wiring into the Runner

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
Cross-session semantic recall with Memory, and versioned binary storage with Artifacts

Day 9 / 15
ADK v2.7.0 (Aug 2026)
Python 3.10+

🎯 Learning Objectives

- Memorize the `BaseMemoryService` contract: `add_session_to_memory`, `add_events_to_memory`, `search_memory`

- Choose between `InMemoryMemoryService`, `VertexAiMemoryBankService`, and `VertexAiRagMemoryService`

- Wire the `load_memory` auto-injected tool and share memory across runners via `Runner(memory_service=...)`

- Save and load versioned binary artifacts via `BaseArtifactService` — `types.Part.from_bytes()`, session vs `user:` namespacing

- Use `context.save_artifact()` / `context.load_artifact()` in callbacks and tools, and exploit v2.7.0's media-returning tools

sections.title: 1. Why this matters
sections.body:
Sessions (Day 08) give your agent a *short-term* memory — the current conversation. But users do not live in one conversation. They come back tomorrow, open a new chat, and expect the agent to remember what was discussed last week. "What did I ask you about Docker last month?" should produce a real answer, not a blank stare. That is the job of the **Memory Service**.

And then there are *files*. A report-generation agent needs to produce a PDF and let the user download it later. An image-editing agent needs to store intermediate versions. A form-filling agent needs to persist a user's saved settings as JSON across sessions. These are binary blobs — too big and too unstructured for state — and they need versioning. That is the job of the **Artifact Service**.

Together, Memory and Artifacts are the two long-term storage systems in ADK. They complement session state (Day 07): state is small, structured, per-session-or-per-user key-value data; memory is unstructured semantic recall across sessions; artifacts are versioned binary files with namespaced access. Knowing which one to reach for — and how to wire them into the Runner — is the difference between a toy demo and a product.

Today we will build all three: an InMemory memory recall loop, a cross-session `load_memory` agent, a PDF artifact save-and-reload pipeline, and a user-scoped settings artifact. We will also cover the v2.7.0 feature that lets tools return media (images, audio) directly in function responses — a small change with big implications for multimodal agents.

sections.title: 2. Core Concepts
sections.body:
Two services, one day. Memory on the left, Artifacts on the right — both plug into the Runner as optional dependencies.

### 2.1 BaseMemoryService — semantic recall across sessions

`BaseMemoryService` at `google.adk.memory.base_memory_service` defines a small abstract API:

```python
class BaseMemoryService(abc.ABC):
    async def add_session_to_memory(self, session: Session) -> None: ...
    async def add_events_to_memory(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, events: list[Event],
    ) -> None: ...        # optional — not every impl supports this
    async def add_memory(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, memory: MemoryEntry,
    ) -> None: ...        # optional
    async def search_memory(
        self, *, app_name: str, user_id: str, query: str,
    ) -> list[SearchMemoryResponse]: ...
```

The typical lifecycle: a user finishes a conversation, you call `add_session_to_memory(session)` to ingest it. Later — possibly in a different session, possibly days later — the user asks a question. The agent calls the `load_memory` tool, which invokes `search_memory(query)`, gets back matching memory snippets, and incorporates them into its response.

Three implementations ship with ADK:

| Service | Persistence | Search method | Use case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `InMemoryMemoryService` | None (process memory) | Basic keyword match | Prototyping, unit tests |
| `VertexAiMemoryBankService` | Google Cloud Agent Platform | Advanced semantic search | Building evolving memories from conversations |
| `VertexAiRagMemoryService` | Google Cloud Knowledge Engine | Vector similarity (RAG) | RAG over raw conversation corpus |

`InMemoryMemoryService` is fine for development — it lets you test the full memory loop without GCP setup. But it does a naive keyword scan, so semantic queries ("what did we say about containers?" matching a conversation about "Docker") will not work. Switch to VertexAi for production-grade semantic recall.

**`VertexAiRagMemoryService`** can be imported from `google.adk.memory` but raises `ImportError` at construction unless `pip install google-adk[gcp]` is installed. Plan for this in your deploy script.

```
MEMORY SERVICE — save then search
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Session A (turn 1-N)
        │
        │  user discusses Python dependency management
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ await memory.add_session_    │  ← ingest completed session
  │   to_memory(session)         │     (call after session ends)
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  Memory store                │
  │  • InMemory (keyword match)  │
  │  • VertexAi Memory Bank      │
  │  • VertexAi RAG (vectors)    │
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │
     ─────────── │ ───────────  (time passes, new session)
                 │
                 ▼
  Session B (turn 1)
        │
        │  user: "what did we say about pip vs poetry?"
        ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Agent calls load_memory      │  ← auto-injected tool
  │   tool → memory.search_      │
  │   memory(query="pip poetry") │
  └──────────────┬───────────────┘
                 │  returns matching memory snippets
                 ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │ Agent synthesizes answer     │
  │ "Last week you preferred     │
  │  poetry for libraries, pip   │
  │  for quick scripts..."       │
  └──────────────────────────────┘
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

💡 Key Concept

The `Runner` accepts a `memory_service=` parameter. **Multiple runners must share the same memory service instance** (or at least the same backing store) for memory to cross agent boundaries. If runner A and runner B each construct their own `InMemoryMemoryService`, they have independent memories. With `VertexAiMemoryBankService`, sharing the same project/resource is sufficient.

### 2.2 The `load_memory` tool — auto-injected recall

The `load_memory` tool at `google.adk.tools` is a pre-built `FunctionTool` that queries the Runner's `memory_service`. Add it to any agent's `tools` list and the LLM can call it to recall past conversations.

```python
from google.adk.tools import load_memory
from google.adk.memory import InMemoryMemoryService

recall_agent = LlmAgent(
    name="recall_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction=(
        "Answer the user's question. If the answer might be in past "
        "conversations, call the 'load_memory' tool with a search query "
        "first, then synthesize your answer from the returned memories."
    ),
    tools=[load_memory],
)

runner = Runner(
    agent=recall_agent,
    app_name="my_app",
    session_service=session_service,
    memory_service=InMemoryMemoryService(),  # ← required for load_memory
)
```

When the LLM calls `load_memory(query="docker containers")`, ADK internally calls `memory_service.search_memory(app_name=..., user_id=..., query="docker containers")`. The returned memories are passed back to the LLM as the tool's function response, which the LLM uses to ground its answer.

**Important**: if you add `load_memory` to an agent's tools but do not configure a `memory_service` on the Runner, the tool call will fail at runtime with a clear error. The two must be wired together.

**`preload_memory_tool`** is a sibling tool that proactively loads relevant memories at the start of each turn (before the LLM even decides whether to query). Use it for agents that should *always* have recent context — for example, a personal assistant that needs to know what you discussed yesterday before responding to today's message.

### 2.3 BaseArtifactService — versioned binary storage

`BaseArtifactService` at `google.adk.artifacts.base_artifact_service` defines the artifact API:

```python
class BaseArtifactService(abc.ABC):
    async def save_artifact(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id, filename, artifact: Part,
    ) -> int: ...   # returns the new version number (starts at 0)

    async def load_artifact(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id, filename,
        version: int | None = None,
    ) -> Part | None: ...   # None → latest

    async def list_artifact_keys(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id,
    ) -> list[str]: ...

    async def list_versions(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id, filename,
    ) -> list[int]: ...

    async def get_artifact_version(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id, filename, version,
    ) -> ArtifactVersion: ...

    async def delete_artifact(
        self, *, app_name, user_id, session_id, filename,
    ) -> None: ...
```

Two implementations:

- **`InMemoryArtifactService`** — `from google.adk.artifacts import InMemoryArtifactService`. Dev/testing only. Stores artifacts in a nested Python dict. Lost on restart.
- **`GcsArtifactService`** — `from google.adk.artifacts import GcsArtifactService`. Production. Stores each version as a distinct GCS object (`gs://bucket/path/file_v0.bin`, `..._v1.bin`, ...). Versioning starts at `0` and increments on every `save_artifact` call. Requires `pip install google-adk[gcp]` and a GCS bucket.

```python
from google.adk.artifacts import GcsArtifactService

gcs_artifacts = GcsArtifactService(bucket_name="my-adk-artifacts-bucket")
```

If no `artifact_service` is configured on the Runner, calling `save_artifact` / `load_artifact` raises `ValueError`. Always wire one up if your tools or callbacks touch artifacts.

```
ARTIFACT SERVICE — versioned binary storage
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  save_artifact("report.pdf", part_v0)   → version 0
  save_artifact("report.pdf", part_v1)   → version 1
  save_artifact("report.pdf", part_v2)   → version 2

  load_artifact("report.pdf")            → version 2 (latest)
  load_artifact("report.pdf", version=0) → version 0 (original)
  load_artifact("report.pdf", version=1) → version 1

  list_versions("report.pdf")            → [0, 1, 2]
  list_artifact_keys()                   → ["report.pdf", "notes.txt", ...]
  delete_artifact("report.pdf")          → removes all versions

  Namespacing:
    "report.pdf"            → session-scoped (app_name, user_id, session_id)
    "user:settings.json"    → user-scoped   (app_name, user_id) — cross-session
    "app:logo.png"          → app-scoped    (app_name) — cross-user

  Representation:
    artifact = types.Part.from_bytes(data=bytes, mime_type="application/pdf")
    # or:
    artifact = types.Part(inline_data=types.Blob(
        mime_type="application/pdf", data=bytes,
    ))
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

### 2.4 Representation and namespacing

**Representation.** Artifacts are `google.genai.types.Part` objects with an `inline_data` field containing a `Blob` (which has `data: bytes` and `mime_type: str`). Two construction patterns:

```python
import google.genai.types as types

# Pattern 1 — convenience classmethod (recommended)
pdf_artifact = types.Part.from_bytes(
    data=pdf_bytes,
    mime_type="application/pdf",
)

# Pattern 2 — explicit construction
pdf_artifact = types.Part(
    inline_data=types.Blob(
        mime_type="application/pdf",
        data=pdf_bytes,
    ),
)

# Reading back:
data: bytes = artifact.inline_data.data
mime: str = artifact.inline_data.mime_type
```

The `mime_type` matters: it tells the LLM (and your UI) how to interpret the bytes. Use standard MIME types — `application/pdf`, `image/png`, `application/json`, `text/plain`, `audio/wav`.

**Namespacing.** The `filename` argument determines scope, using the same prefix convention as session state (Day 07):

| Filename pattern | Scope | Access |
|---|---|---|
| `"report.pdf"` (no prefix) | Session-scoped | `(app_name, user_id, session_id)` — only this session |
| `"user:settings.json"` | User-scoped | `(app_name, user_id)` — all sessions for this user |
| `"app:logo.png"` | App-scoped | `(app_name)` — all users |

Session-scoped is the default — artifacts are tied to the conversation that created them. Use `user:` for cross-session files (user preferences, saved drafts, profile pictures). Use `app:` for shared assets (branding, templates).

**Context-based access.** You rarely call `save_artifact` / `load_artifact` on the service directly. Instead, use the `CallbackContext` (in callbacks) or `ToolContext` (in tools) convenience methods:

```python
async def my_tool(tool_context: ToolContext, ...) -> dict:
    # Save an artifact — version number is returned
    version = await tool_context.save_artifact(
        filename="report.pdf",
        artifact=pdf_part,
    )
    # The next event's actions.artifact_delta will be
    # {"report.pdf": version} — tracked automatically.

    # Load latest version
    part = await tool_context.load_artifact(filename="report.pdf")

    # List all artifact keys in scope
    keys = await tool_context.list_artifacts()
```

The framework tracks saves via `actions.artifact_delta` (a `dict[str, int]` mapping filename → version), exactly like `state_delta` tracks state changes. Downstream agents can inspect `artifact_delta` to know what files were produced.

🚀 Pro Tip

**v2.7.0 feature**: tools can now return MEDIA (images, audio) directly in their function response. A tool that generates an image can return `types.Part.from_bytes(data=..., mime_type="image/png")` as part of its response dict, and the LLM will see the image — no need to save it as an artifact first. This is huge for multimodal agents (image generation, screenshot analysis, audio transcription). The media is forwarded on Gemini, Anthropic, LiteLLM, Apigee, and OCI alike.

sections.title: 5. Visual — Memory + Artifact services
sections.body:
The pre-generated matplotlib diagram shows the two services side by side, their implementations, key methods, and how they connect to the Runner. Use it as a reference card.

```python
from IPython.display import Image, display
display(Image(filename="images/day09_memory_artifacts.png"))
```

💡 Key Concept

The Runner is the hub. Session, Memory, and Artifact services are the three spokes — each optional, each pluggable, each with its own scope and persistence model. Most production agents configure all three: Session for the current conversation, Memory for cross-session recall, Artifacts for generated files.

sections.title: 6. Four Progressive Examples
sections.body:
Two examples for Memory, two for Artifacts. By the end you will have patterns for cross-session recall and versioned file storage.

1. **Example 1** — InMemory memory: save a session, search in a later session
2. **Example 2** — `load_memory` tool: agent recalls past conversations
3. **Example 3** — PDF artifact: generate a report, save, reload
4. **Example 4** — User-scoped JSON settings artifact

Example 1: InMemory Memory — Save Then Search

Ingest a completed session, then search_memory in a later session.

The simplest memory loop: two sessions for the same user. Session A discusses a topic; we call `add_session_to_memory` to ingest it. Session B (a brand-new session, same user) calls `search_memory` and gets back snippets from session A.

We use `InMemoryMemoryService` — no GCP setup required, perfect for development. The search is keyword-based (not semantic), so the query must contain words that appeared in the original conversation. Switch to `VertexAiMemoryBankService` for production-grade semantic search.

The key insight: memory is keyed by `(app_name, user_id)`. Session B does not need to know session A's ID — it just needs the same `user_id`. This is what makes memory "cross-session": the user's identity is the join key, not the session ID.

```python
# agent.py — Example 1: InMemory memory save + search
import asyncio
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.memory import InMemoryMemoryService
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.genai import types

root_agent = Agent(
    name="memory_demo_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    instruction="You are a helpful assistant. Answer concisely.",
)

async def memory_loop():
    session_svc = InMemorySessionService()
    memory_svc = InMemoryMemoryService()

    runner = Runner(
        agent=root_agent,
        app_name="demo_app",
        session_service=session_svc,
        memory_service=memory_svc,
    )

    # ── Session A: discuss Docker ───────────────────────────
    sess_a = await session_svc.create_session(
        app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice",
    )
    msg = types.Content(
        role="user",
        parts=[types.Part.from_text(
            text="I'm learning Docker. What's the difference between "
                 "an image and a container?"
        )],
    )
    async for _ in runner.run_async(
        user_id="alice", session_id=sess_a.id, new_message=msg,
    ):
        pass  # consume events

    # Ingest session A into memory
    await memory_svc.add_session_to_memory(sess_a)
    print(f"[Session A] ingested into memory")

    # ── Session B: brand new session, same user ─────────────
    sess_b = await session_svc.create_session(
        app_name="demo_app", user_id="alice",
    )
    print(f"[Session B] new session created (no shared state with A)")

    # Search memory for Docker-related content
    results = await memory_svc.search_memory(
        app_name="demo_app",
        user_id="alice",
        query="Docker image container",
    )
    print(f"[Session B] search_memory returned {len(results)} match(es)")
    for r in results:
        print(f"  - {r.memory_entry.text[:80]}...")

# asyncio.run(memory_loop())
print("Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(memory_loop()) to execute.")
```

**Output**

```text
Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(memory_loop()) to execute.

Expected output:
[Session A] ingested into memory
[Session B] new session created (no shared state with A)
[Session B] search_memory returned 1 match(es)
  - An image is a read-only template with the app and dependencies.
    A container is a running instance of an image...
```

⚠️ Important

`InMemoryMemoryService` does a naive substring/keyword scan. If session A said "Docker" but your search query is "containerization technology", it will NOT match. For semantic recall, use `VertexAiMemoryBankService` or `VertexAiRagMemoryService` — they embed both the conversation and the query into vector space and match by cosine similarity.

Example 2: Cross-Session Recall with load_memory Tool

Agent autonomously queries past conversations via the load_memory tool.

Example 1 showed the manual `search_memory` call. In production, you do not call it yourself — the agent does, via the `load_memory` tool. The LLM decides when to query memory based on the user's question.

The setup: add `load_memory` to the agent's `tools` list, and wire a `memory_service` into the Runner. The LLM's instruction tells it to use `load_memory` when the answer "might be in past conversations." When the LLM emits a `function_call` to `load_memory`, ADK calls `memory_service.search_memory(query=...)` internally and returns the results as the function response.

The magic: the agent has no idea *what* is in memory. It just knows it has a tool to search past conversations. The LLM writes the search query based on the user's question, gets back snippets, and synthesizes an answer. This is a clean separation of concerns — the memory store is opaque to the agent, the agent is opaque to the memory store.

We also show `preload_memory_tool` — a sibling tool that proactively loads relevant memories at the start of every turn, before the LLM decides whether to query. Useful for personal-assistant agents that should always have recent context.

```python
# agent.py — Example 2: load_memory tool for autonomous recall
import asyncio
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.memory import InMemoryMemoryService
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.adk.tools import load_memory
from google.genai import types

recall_agent = Agent(
    name="recall_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Answers questions, recalling past conversations when relevant.",
    instruction=(
        "You are a helpful assistant with access to the user's past "
        "conversations via the 'load_memory' tool.\n"
        "\n"
        "When the user asks about something you've discussed before "
        "(e.g. 'what did we say about...?', 'last week you mentioned...'), "
        "call 'load_memory' with a search query first. Then synthesize "
        "your answer from the returned memories.\n"
        "\n"
        "If load_memory returns nothing relevant, say you don't recall "
        "and answer from your general knowledge."
    ),
    tools=[load_memory],
)

# Shared services — memory must persist across sessions, so we
# construct the service ONCE and reuse it for all runners.
session_svc = InMemorySessionService()
memory_svc = InMemoryMemoryService()

runner = Runner(
    agent=recall_agent,
    app_name="recall_app",
    session_service=session_svc,
    memory_service=memory_svc,  # ← load_memory tool needs this
)

async def seed_and_recall():
    # Session 1: user tells the agent about their project
    s1 = await session_svc.create_session(
        app_name="recall_app", user_id="alice",
    )
    msg1 = types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part.from_text(
        text="I'm building a RAG pipeline with LangChain and Pinecone. "
             "The main challenge is chunk size — 512 tokens seems too small."
    )])
    async for _ in runner.run_async(
        user_id="alice", session_id=s1.id, new_message=msg1,
    ):
        pass
    await memory_svc.add_session_to_memory(s1)
    print("[Session 1] seeded memory with RAG pipeline discussion")

    # Session 2 (NEW): user asks a recall question
    s2 = await session_svc.create_session(
        app_name="recall_app", user_id="alice",
    )
    msg2 = types.Content(role="user", parts=[types.Part.from_text(
        text="What chunk size did I say I was using for my RAG pipeline?"
    )])
    print("\n[Session 2] user asks recall question...")
    async for event in runner.run_async(
        user_id="alice", session_id=s2.id, new_message=msg2,
    ):
        if event.is_final_response() and event.content:
            print(f"Agent: {event.content.parts[0].text}")

# asyncio.run(seed_and_recall())
print("Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(seed_and_recall()) to execute.")
```

**Output**

```text
Demo defined — uncomment asyncio.run(seed_and_recall()) to execute.

Expected output:
[Session 1] seeded memory with RAG pipeline discussion

[Session 2] user asks recall question...
[recall_agent] calling tool: load_memory(query='RAG pipeline chunk size')
  → 1 memory match returned
Agent: In our previous conversation, you mentioned using 512-token chunks
for your RAG pipeline with LangChain and Pinecone, and noted that 512
seemed too small for your use case.
```

💡 Key Concept

The `load_memory` tool is the bridge between the agent and the memory service. The agent does not need to know *how* memories are stored or searched — it just calls the tool with a query string. Swap `InMemoryMemoryService` for `VertexAiRagMemoryService` and the agent's code does not change; only the quality of search results improves.

Example 3: PDF Artifact — Generate, Save, Reload

Generate a report as PDF bytes, save as a versioned artifact, reload next turn.

Now to artifacts. A report-generation agent produces a PDF. We save it as an artifact via `tool_context.save_artifact(filename="weekly_report.pdf", artifact=pdf_part)`. The service returns a version number (starting at 0). Next turn — or next session — we reload it via `tool_context.load_artifact(filename="weekly_report.pdf")` (defaults to latest version) or `load_artifact(filename="weekly_report.pdf", version=0)` for the original.

We use `types.Part.from_bytes(data=pdf_bytes, mime_type="application/pdf")` to construct the artifact. The `mime_type` is critical — it tells consumers (the LLM, your UI, downstream tools) how to interpret the bytes.

The example uses `InMemoryArtifactService` for simplicity. In production, swap to `GcsArtifactService(bucket_name="...")` — each version becomes a distinct GCS object (`gs://bucket/.../weekly_report_v0.pdf`, `..._v1.pdf`, etc.). Versioning starts at 0 and increments on every save.

The simulated output shows three turns: generate + save (version 0), regenerate + save (version 1), then reload version 0 to compare. The `list_artifacts()` call shows all keys in scope; `list_versions()` shows all versions of one key.

```python
# agent.py — Example 3: PDF artifact save/load
import asyncio
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.artifacts import InMemoryArtifactService
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.genai import types

def generate_weekly_report(topic: str, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Generate a weekly report PDF about the given topic and save it.

    Args:
        topic (str): The topic for this week's report.
    """
    # In production, use a real PDF library (reportlab, weasyprint, etc.)
    # Here we simulate with placeholder bytes.
    pdf_bytes = f"%PDF-1.4\nWeekly Report: {topic}\nGenerated at turn {tool_context.state.get('turn_count', '?')}\n%%EOF".encode()
    artifact = types.Part.from_bytes(
        data=pdf_bytes, mime_type="application/pdf",
    )
    # save_artifact returns the version number (starts at 0)
    version = tool_context.save_artifact(
        filename="weekly_report.pdf", artifact=artifact,
    )
    return {
        "status": "generated",
        "filename": "weekly_report.pdf",
        "version": version,
        "size_bytes": len(pdf_bytes),
    }

def load_previous_report(version: int | None, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Load a previously saved weekly report PDF.

    Args:
        version (int|None): Version to load. None = latest.
    """
    part = tool_context.load_artifact(
        filename="weekly_report.pdf", version=version,
    )
    if part is None:
        return {"status": "not_found", "filename": "weekly_report.pdf"}
    return {
        "status": "loaded",
        "filename": "weekly_report.pdf",
        "mime_type": part.inline_data.mime_type,
        "size_bytes": len(part.inline_data.data),
        "preview": part.inline_data.data[:80].decode("utf-8", errors="replace"),
    }

root_agent = Agent(
    name="report_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Generates and retrieves weekly PDF reports.",
    instruction=(
        "You generate and retrieve weekly reports. Use 'generate_weekly_report' "
        "to create a new report (it saves as a versioned artifact). Use "
        "'load_previous_report' with version=None for the latest, or a specific "
        "version number to retrieve an older one."
    ),
    tools=[generate_weekly_report, load_previous_report],
)

session_svc = InMemorySessionService()
artifact_svc = InMemoryArtifactService()

runner = Runner(
    agent=root_agent,
    app_name="report_app",
    session_service=session_svc,
    artifact_service=artifact_svc,  # ← required for save/load_artifact
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Artifact service: {type(artifact_svc).__name__}")
print(f"Tools: generate_weekly_report, load_previous_report")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: report_agent
Artifact service: InMemoryArtifactService
Tools: generate_weekly_report, load_previous_report
```

```python
# Run three turns: generate v0, generate v1, reload v0
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with report_agent.

>>> Generate a report about Q3 sales.
[report_agent] calling tool: generate_weekly_report(topic='Q3 sales')
  → saved weekly_report.pdf version 0 (47 bytes)
Report generated and saved as weekly_report.pdf (version 0).

>>> Now update it with Q3 marketing data too.
[report_agent] calling tool: generate_weekly_report(topic='Q3 sales and marketing')
  → saved weekly_report.pdf version 1 (62 bytes)
Updated report saved as version 1. The previous version (0) is still available.

>>> Show me the original version.
[report_agent] calling tool: load_previous_report(version=0)
  → loaded weekly_report.pdf v0 (47 bytes, application/pdf)
  preview: %PDF-1.4
Weekly Report: Q3 sales
Generated at turn 1
%%EOF
Here's the original v0 report. It covers Q3 sales only; v1 adds marketing.
```

🚀 Pro Tip

`save_artifact` returns the version number — capture it! Downstream code can then load a specific version with `load_artifact(filename, version=N)`. Without version control, every save overwrites and you lose history. The artifact service is the only place in ADK that gives you free, automatic versioning — use it.

Example 4: User-Scoped Settings Artifact

Save user preferences as a JSON artifact with the user: prefix — cross-session.

Artifacts are not just for big files. Small structured data — user settings, profile data, saved form drafts — also benefits from artifact storage, especially when you want versioning. A `user:settings.json` artifact is cross-session (the `user:` prefix) and versioned (every save creates a new version), making it perfect for "undo last settings change" features.

The pattern: serialize settings to JSON bytes, wrap in `types.Part.from_bytes(data=..., mime_type="application/json")`, save with `user:settings.json` filename. Load with the same filename; parse the JSON bytes back to a dict.

Why use an artifact instead of session state (Day 07)? Two reasons: (1) versioning — you can roll back to last week's settings; (2) size — state is meant for small values, artifacts for anything that could be large. A 50KB JSON document is fine as an artifact but bloated as state.

v2.7.0 bonus: the Jinja2 `{{ artifact("user:settings.json") }}` helper inlines an artifact's text content into an instruction. So you can write an instruction like `"The user's saved settings are: {{ artifact('user:settings.json') }}"` and ADK loads the artifact and injects its content at render time. This is the cleanest way to make instructions adapt to saved user data.

```python
# agent.py — Example 4: User-scoped settings artifact (JSON)
import json
from google.adk.agents.llm_agent import Agent
from google.adk.artifacts import InMemoryArtifactService
from google.adk.runners import Runner
from google.adk.sessions import InMemorySessionService
from google.adk.tools.tool_context import ToolContext
from google.genai import types

def save_settings(settings: dict, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Save the user's settings as a versioned JSON artifact.

    The user: prefix makes this cross-session. Each call creates a new
    version — previous settings are preserved for rollback.

    Args:
        settings (dict): Settings dict, e.g. {"theme": "dark", "lang": "en"}.
    """
    payload = json.dumps(settings, indent=2).encode("utf-8")
    artifact = types.Part.from_bytes(
        data=payload, mime_type="application/json",
    )
    version = tool_context.save_artifact(
        filename="user:settings.json", artifact=artifact,
    )
    return {
        "status": "saved",
        "filename": "user:settings.json",
        "version": version,
        "settings": settings,
    }

def load_settings(version: int | None, tool_context: ToolContext) -> dict:
    """Load saved settings. version=None for latest, or a specific version.

    Args:
        version (int|None): Version to load. None = latest.
    """
    part = tool_context.load_artifact(
        filename="user:settings.json", version=version,
    )
    if part is None:
        return {"status": "not_found", "settings": {}}
    data = json.loads(part.inline_data.data.decode("utf-8"))
    return {
        "status": "loaded",
        "version": version,
        "settings": data,
    }

root_agent = Agent(
    name="settings_agent",
    model="gemini-2.0-flash",
    description="Manages user settings as a versioned JSON artifact.",
    instruction=(
        "You manage the user's settings. Use 'save_settings' to save a "
        "settings dict (this creates a new version each time). Use "
        "'load_settings' with version=None for the latest, or a number "
        "to retrieve an older version. Help the user understand what "
        "changed between versions."
    ),
    tools=[save_settings, load_settings],
)

session_svc = InMemorySessionService()
artifact_svc = InMemoryArtifactService()

runner = Runner(
    agent=root_agent,
    app_name="settings_app",
    session_service=session_svc,
    artifact_service=artifact_svc,
)

print(f"Agent: {root_agent.name}")
print(f"Artifact namespacing: user:settings.json → cross-session for one user")
print(f"Each save creates a new version — full rollback history available")
```

**Output**

```text
Agent: settings_agent
Artifact namespacing: user:settings.json → cross-session for one user
Each save creates a new version — full rollback history available
```

```python
# Run the agent — note settings persist across sessions (user: prefix)
# !adk run my_first_agent
```

**Output**

```text
Welcome to ADK! You are now interacting with settings_agent.

>>> Save my settings: theme dark, language English.
[settings_agent] calling tool: save_settings(settings={'theme':'dark','language':'en'})
  → saved user:settings.json version 0
Settings saved (version 0). Use 'load settings' to retrieve them later.

>>> Actually, change theme to light.
[settings_agent] calling tool: save_settings(settings={'theme':'light','language':'en'})
  → saved user:settings.json version 1
Updated (version 1). The dark-theme version (0) is still available for rollback.

>>> What were my previous settings?
[settings_agent] calling tool: load_settings(version=0)
  → loaded user:settings.json v0: {'theme':'dark','language':'en'}
Your previous settings (v0) had theme=dark. You changed to light in v1.
```

💡 Key Concept

The `user:` prefix on the filename is what makes this artifact cross-session. Without it, the artifact would be session-scoped and the user would lose their settings every time they started a new chat. The prefix convention is the same as for session state (Day 07) — `user:` for cross-session, `app:` for cross-user, no prefix for session-only.

sections.title: Day 9 Summary
sections.body:
📌 Key Takeaways

- **Memory Service** gives agents cross-session semantic recall. API: `add_session_to_memory`, `add_events_to_memory`, `search_memory`. Three impls: `InMemoryMemoryService` (keyword, dev), `VertexAiMemoryBankService` (semantic, prod), `VertexAiRagMemoryService` (vector RAG).

- **The `load_memory` tool (in `google.adk.tools`) is auto-injected — add it to `tools=[...]` and the LLM calls it to query past conversations. Requires `Runner(memory_service=...)` to be wired.**

- **Memory is keyed by `(app_name, user_id)`** — not by session_id. This is what makes it cross-session. Multiple runners must share the same memory service instance (or backing store) to share memory.

- **Artifact Service** gives versioned binary storage. API: `save_artifact` (returns version, starts at 0), `load_artifact` (version=None for latest), `list_artifact_keys`, `list_versions`, `delete_artifact`.

- **Artifacts are `google.genai.types.Part` objects with `inline_data` (`Blob` with `data: bytes` and `mime_type: str`). Construct with `types.Part.from_bytes(data=..., mime_type=...)`.**

- **Namespacing uses the same prefix convention as state: `"file.pdf"` (session), `"user:file.json"` (cross-session), `"app:logo.png"` (cross-user). Use `context.save_artifact()` / `context.load_artifact()` in tools and callbacks — the framework tracks saves via `actions.artifact_delta`.**

- **v2.7.0:** tools can return MEDIA (images, audio) directly in function responses via `types.Part.from_bytes` in the return dict. Supported on Gemini, Anthropic, LiteLLM, Apigee, OCI. Also: Jinja2 `{{ artifact("name") }}` helper inlines artifact text content into instructions.
